pll1d26c6-d1e3501.summary: Applies the same to the Spirit: he is properly called Gift of God, though there are many other gifts, being Gift by eternal and immutable property as the Son is Son. He is called Gift as he is called Holy Spirit, both relatively and by the same relation, though it appears more in 'Gift.'
claims: The Spirit is Gift by eternal property.
'Holy Spirit' and 'Gift' express the same relation.

pll1d26c6-d1e3504.summary: Cites De Trinitate V: the Spirit, not the Trinity but in the Trinity, is said relatively as Spirit of Father and Son; the relation appears in 'Gift of God,' since he proceeds from both. He is the ineffable communion of Father and Son, and bears as proper the name common to both, since each is spirit and holy, so that their communion is signified by a name common to both.
claims: The Spirit is the ineffable communion of Father and Son.
He bears as proper a name common to both.

pll1d26c6-d1e3522.summary: Concludes that the Spirit is properly called Gift, both names are relative, and he bears as proper a name common to Father and Son taken separately. When Father or Son is called spirit or holy, it is said not relatively but substantially.
claims: 'Spirit' or 'holy' said of Father or Son is substantial.

pl-l1d26c6.summary: Applies the same to the Spirit: he is properly called Gift of God, though there are many gifts, being Gift by eternal and immutable property as the Son is Son by property. 'Gift' and 'Holy Spirit' are said by the same relation, though it appears more in 'Gift.' Augustine: the Spirit is the ineffable communion of Father and Son and bears as proper the name common to both (both are spirit and holy), so that the common name signifies their communion. When Father or Son is called spirit or holy, it is said substantially, not relatively.
claims: The Spirit is properly Gift by an eternal, immutable property.
'Holy Spirit' and 'Gift' are said by the same relation.
The relation appears in 'Gift' but not in 'Holy Spirit.'
The Spirit is the ineffable communion of Father and Son.
He bears as proper the name common to Father and Son.
When said of Father or Son, 'spirit' and 'holy' are substantial, not relative.
